title: How Do You Know If a Book Is in the Public Domain?
excerpt: A book being old does not automatically mean it is in the public domain. A book being free online does not automatically mean it is in the public domain either.

content:
If you only want to read a copy, the distinction may not affect you much. If you want to republish, adapt, distribute, teach from, or sell a version of the work, it matters a lot.

What “public domain” means

A work in the public domain is not protected by copyright, so copyright permission is not required for uses that would otherwise be controlled by the copyright owner. Works can enter the public domain because copyright expired, because the material was never eligible for copyright, or for other legal reasons.

For U.S. works, start with the publication date

As of 2026, the U.S. Copyright Office states that works published in the United States before January 1, 1931 are in the public domain because their copyright terms have expired. Older publication periods have their own rules and historical formalities, so do not apply a single modern formula to every old book.

Modern works usually last much longer

For most works created on or after January 1, 1978, U.S. copyright generally lasts for the life of the author plus 70 years. Anonymous, pseudonymous, and works made for hire generally use a term of 95 years from publication or 120 years from creation, whichever ends first.

Edition rights can complicate things

The underlying text of a nineteenth-century novel may be public domain while a modern translation, introduction, cover design, annotations, or edited edition is still protected. If you plan to reuse a digital file, check what exactly that file contains.

Do not infer rights from availability

The Library of Congress explicitly notes that material appearing on its website is not automatically free for unrestricted reuse. Rights vary by item. Likewise, a random PDF on the open web tells you almost nothing about whether the uploader had permission to post it.

Use reputable rights information

Project Gutenberg focuses on works that are not restricted by U.S. copyright and provides license information with its ebooks. The U.S. Copyright Office publishes guidance on copyright duration. Libraries and archives often attach rights statements to individual items.

If you are curating or selling, verify before publishing

Platforms that allow people to publish collections need the same caution. Kahana, for example, permits public-domain and appropriately licensed works but requires creators to confirm that they have the right to share everything in a public, unlisted, or monetized hub and to include required attribution or license information.

When commercial use, international distribution, a newer edition, or uncertain authorship is involved, the rules can become more complicated. Treat this article as a starting checklist rather than legal advice.

The safest habit is simple: identify the exact work and edition, check the relevant jurisdiction and date, read the rights statement, and document what you relied on before you republish anything.
